mcqs.question: What does implementing level filtering as a Chain of Responsibility actually buy you over a single if/elif ladder inside Logger?
options: It guarantees log records are delivered in the order they were generated
It makes each individual log call run measurably faster than a direct comparison
It removes the need for a LogLevel enum entirely
Adding a new level or per-level side effects doesn't require modifying Logger, only the chain of handlers
mcqs.explanation: The pattern's benefit is extensibility, not raw speed — a single comparison is just as fast as walking a chain. The win is that new levels or handler-specific behavior slot into the chain without touching Logger. It still needs a LogLevel enum to order the handlers, and ordering guarantees are a separate, unrelated concern from filtering.

mcqs.question: Why do most real logging frameworks use a named-logger registry instead of a single global Logger Singleton?
options: A registry is required because Singletons can't be implemented in most languages
Global loggers are slower at formatting log messages than named ones
A single global logger makes per-module level overrides and clean test isolation harder, since all state is shared everywhere
Named loggers eliminate the need for an Appender interface
mcqs.explanation: The registry pattern (getLogger by name) keeps the convenience of 'always get the same instance for a name' while letting each named logger carry its own level and appenders — something a single global object can't do without extra plumbing, and which also makes tests easier to isolate. Singletons are perfectly implementable in any mainstream language; this is a design trade-off, not a technical limitation, and it has nothing to do with formatting speed or the Appender interface.

mcqs.question: In an async logging design, why does the bounded queue need an explicit 'full policy' rather than just growing to fit demand?
options: Queues in most languages have a hard, unconfigurable maximum size
A full policy is only needed if the writer thread crashes
Without a bound, the queue can grow unbounded under load, trading the caller-latency problem for an unbounded-memory problem — the full policy defines what happens once a real limit is hit
It's required so multiple writer threads can drain the queue in parallel
mcqs.explanation: An unbounded queue just relocates the problem: instead of the caller blocking on I/O, the process now risks running out of memory if producers permanently outrun the writer. A bounded queue forces an explicit choice — block, drop, or discard-oldest — for what happens at that limit. Queue sizing is configurable, this applies whether or not the writer thread has crashed, and the design here uses one writer thread, not several.

mcqs.question: A logging call's formatter throws an exception on malformed input, and that exception propagates into the business logic that called logger.info(). What's the correct fix?
options: Wrap every appender and formatter call so failures are caught and reported internally, never re-thrown into the caller
Switch to synchronous logging so failures happen predictably
Remove the formatter and log raw LogRecord objects instead
Have the caller wrap every logging call in its own try/except block
mcqs.explanation: The fix belongs inside the logging framework, not the caller — logging must be allowed to fail silently from the outside, since it's a side effect, not core business logic. Making callers defensively wrap every log call is exactly the burden the framework should absorb instead. Switching sync/async or dropping the formatter doesn't address the actual bug, which is an unguarded call site.

mcqs.question: In an async logger with one shared writer thread, why is it a problem if that thread calls each appender synchronously, one after another?
options: It has no downside as long as the queue itself is bounded
It doubles the memory used per LogRecord
A single slow appender (e.g. a network call) blocks the shared writer thread, stalling every other appender and every queued record behind it
It prevents the formatter from being reused across appenders
mcqs.explanation: The writer thread is a single shared resource in this design; if it waits on one slow, blocking appender, nothing else it's responsible for makes progress, including fast appenders and every other queued record. Bounding the queue doesn't fix this — it's a throughput problem, not a memory one, and it has no effect on formatter reuse.
